title: Technology and architecture
lede: Rewind combines a browser PWA, a modular Node server, relational metadata and private media storage to turn group contributions into a released film.
intro: This map follows the 20 October 2026 refactor checkout. The code takes precedence over older report models: real accounts are the product, the synthetic Demo is removed, and hosted dev uses PostgreSQL. Deployment diagrams describe the repository configuration; release completion remains tracked separately.

sections.title: The technology stack
sections.summary: One root package.json declares the client and server dependencies; TypeScript is compiled before the server runs.
paragraphs: The web client is an Expo export built from React Native components. The PWA adds a manifest and a project-owned service worker. It caches the public shell and matching bundles; it does not cache private API/media responses or queue writes while offline.

rows: Share components and capture adapters across web and retained native development paths.
Client types and compiled server JavaScript.
Node `>=22.13.0` required; `.nvmrc` is `22.23.3`; Docker runtime is `26.10.0`
Built-in `node:http` and `node:sqlite`; no Express routing layer. These are declared versions, not a live host probe.
Shared synchronous SQL surface through a worker-thread adapter. SQLite is bundled with Node.
Private object storage and verified managed-login identity.
VAPID web push received by the service worker; Expo push remains disabled.
Docker installs FFmpeg `8.1.2-r0`; web image uses nginx `1.31.6`
Probe and compile media; serve the static export and proxy the API.
Installable shell with build-specific cache identity and generic push notifications.

qa.q: Is the PWA a separate application?
qa.a: No. It installs the Expo web export. The manifest and service worker add browser installation, shell caching and web push.

qa.q: Does the PWA work fully offline?
qa.a: The public shell can open offline. Group reads, sign-in, uploads and chat still require the server; private responses and pending writes are not cached.

sections.title: Logical layers
sections.summary: Presentation, application rules and infrastructure are separate code responsibilities inside one application deployment.

visuals.title: From user intent to durable state

layers.label: Presentation
layers.detail: React Native screens collect input and render server state. Shared UI tokens and primitives keep feature screens consistent.

layers.label: Client contracts
layers.detail: src/domain holds framework-free types and policy helpers. Auth, capture, chat and reminder clients translate HTTP responses into those contracts.

layers.label: HTTP boundary
layers.detail: http.ts dispatches to route tables. Routes bound bodies, validate transport and sessions, then call application functions.

layers.label: Application rules
layers.detail: Membership, quota, lifecycle, chat and release checks decide what may happen. The pure cycle engine is distinct from database-backed orchestration.

layers.label: Infrastructure
layers.detail: db.ts and schema.ts manage relational state; media adapters and FFmpeg handle bytes; Cognito and web-push providers handle external protocols.

visuals.caption: These are logical dependencies, not five network services. SQL calls remain in application modules; this is not a claim of a fully isolated repository layer.

paragraphs: Feature modules share transactions and one release unit. The default CLI starts HTTP, the cycle/media scheduler and configured reminder loop. FFmpeg child processes and the PostgreSQL I/O thread do not turn these modules into independently deployed microservices.

The import guard keeps `src/domain` and the pure cycle engine free of non-relative imports. It is a focused static rule, not proof that every dependency obeys a strict architectural layer. See [design decisions](decisions.html#monolith) and [analysis to design](analysis-design.html).

qa.q: Why call this a modular monolith?
qa.a: Features are separate TypeScript modules but share one server deployment and relational state. They call functions directly rather than communicating through service APIs.
The server is authoritative for membership, quota and publication. Client checks guide the user but do not authorise a request.

sections.title: Packages and the server refactor
sections.summary: The presentation packages map to feature modules; they are not separate npm packages.

visuals.title: Four members, five modelling packages

items.label: Access
items.detail: Sign-in, profiles, private groups, memberships and invitations. Code: auth/* and groups/*.

items.label: Capture
items.detail: Photos/videos, upload intent, allowance and correction. Code: contributions/*, media/* and capture hooks.

items.label: Cycle
items.detail: Collection boundaries, durable compilation and release publication. Code: cycles/*, jobs/* and ffmpeg.ts.

items.label: Archive
items.detail: Premiere, released films, own clips and capability-based playback/download. Code: archive/* and archive-routes.ts.

items.label: Participation
items.detail: Prompt/timezone settings, web-push reminders and private chat. Code: reminders/*, chat/* and realtime/*.

visuals.caption: The fixed ownership split is the presentation assumption. It does not assert historical authorship of each commit.

qa.q: What changed in the HTTP refactor?
qa.a: The large transport module was split into route tables and shared route helpers. http.ts now composes them; the API remains one server.

qa.q: Does a report package equal a deployable component?
qa.a: No. Access, capture, cycle, participation and archive organise the models and explanation. Implementation boundaries are folders and functions within the shared application.

sections.title: Deployment and external services
sections.summary: The declared hosted path is browser/PWA → CloudFront → nginx → Node on a Lightsail host.

visuals.title: The hosted request path

steps.label: Browser / PWA
steps.detail: Loads the Expo web export and sends same-origin /api requests.

steps.label: CloudFront
steps.detail: Redirects viewers to HTTPS and injects the configured origin secret. The declared connection to the host origin is HTTP.

steps.label: nginx
steps.detail: Serves web files, strips /api before proxying, disables API buffering/cache and forwards the origin proof.

steps.label: Node container
steps.detail: Calls PostgreSQL, S3, Cognito and web-push providers. Compose supplies persistent local mounts for runtime data and temporary media.

steps.label: External services
steps.detail: PostgreSQL holds relational state, S3 holds private media and Cognito proves identity. Node calls each service; the browser also redirects to Cognito and performs approved incoming S3 PUTs.

visuals.caption: The final box groups parallel service connections, not a chain between providers. nginx is the application proxy in deploy/compose.yaml; this view follows the checked-in configuration.

rows: Hosted relational data over verified TLS, with an environment binding.
An approved presigned PUT uploads incoming bytes. Node verifies/materialises them for processing and authorised serving, then stores processed clips and films.
Managed Login redirects the browser; Node exchanges the code and verifies identity before issuing a Rewind session.
A durable outbox supplies generic reminder notifications.
Local browser → local proxy → Node → SQLite/disk
make run-real serves localhost:8090 with short cycles; it exercises the same real-account application.

paragraphs: Terraform declares isolated dev/release hosts, origins, storage and Cognito pools. Hosted dev has PostgreSQL cutover enabled. In the inspected configuration, release database provisioning is enabled but cutover is false. [#230](https://github.com/Collaboration95/rewind-app/issues/230), [#504](https://github.com/Collaboration95/rewind-app/issues/504) and [#515](https://github.com/Collaboration95/rewind-app/issues/515) remain open as checked on 20 October; this page does not claim release is operational. See [AWS setup](aws.html).

qa.a: The declared CloudFront custom origin is HTTP. The runtime trusts forwarded HTTPS only with the configured origin secret; a forwarded protocol header alone is insufficient.
The default configuration has one runtime. SSE fan-out, media grants, rate buckets and identity caches are process-local; more replicas would need coordination or routing changes.

sections.title: Request path: upload a contribution
sections.summary: An upload intent reserves allowance before S3 transfer; completion verifies the exact object before registering the contribution.

steps.label: Reserve
steps.detail: The server validates the real session, selected membership, cycle and remaining allowance. An idempotent intent records an expiring reservation.

steps.label: Transfer
steps.detail: The browser uploads to the approved incoming key with bound headers. A storage write does not yet publish a contribution.

steps.label: Complete
steps.detail: The client supplies versionId. The server pins and verifies object metadata/bytes, rechecks authority, and atomically creates quota usage, contribution and clip-job receipts.

steps.label: Process
steps.detail: The processing pipeline normalises the clip/photo, verifies its output and stores the result. The client uses job status to show queued, processing, sealed or failed.

paragraphs: The runtime paths are `POST /real/groups/:groupId/upload-intents`, `POST .../:intentId/complete` and `POST .../:intentId/reconcile`; the web proxy adds the `/api` prefix. Reconciliation recovers a transfer whose completion response was lost. Repeating a completed intent returns its existing receipt.

The disk path sends bytes through `POST /contributions/upload/source`, then registers them through `/contributions/upload` and processes the clip job. Server probing supplies trusted metadata. The request body, captured dimensions or a client-generated ID never establish ownership by themselves. See [database allowance and integrity](database.html#integrity).

qa.q: What if a retry arrives twice?
qa.a: Intent uniqueness and request hashes distinguish a safe replay from a conflicting request. Completion stores the contribution and job receipt in the same transaction as consumed quota.

qa.q: Can a successful S3 upload bypass quota?
qa.a: No. S3 grants byte transfer only. The application rechecks quota, membership, cycle and exact object version before it registers the contribution.

sections.title: Request path: play a film
sections.summary: The server advertises a short-lived media grant, then rechecks authority and integrity when the player uses it.

visuals.title: From Archive entry to video bytes

steps.label: Request film
steps.detail: The signed-in member requests a released film. The route checks selected membership, release state and the recorded output.

steps.label: Issue grant
steps.detail: MediaCapabilities binds the grant to a session hash, group, job, purpose and exact output. It returns /media/access/<token>.

steps.label: Resolve
steps.detail: The server checks expiry, stored session, current selected membership, published release and unchanged job output. A different presented session is rejected.

steps.label: Verify and stream
steps.detail: The server verifies a bounded snapshot from disk or S3, rechecks the grant and serves GET/HEAD or Range bytes with no-store. Download grants add an attachment filename.

paragraphs: The URL contains neither the application session token nor an object-store path. A media element can use the grant without attaching an app cookie; the server still checks the issuing session in SQL. It is a temporary bearer capability and must be treated as private.

The refactor removes legacy direct film/clip download routes. S3 remains private; playback is mediated by the server so revocation, membership changes and output-integrity checks still apply. See [the media decision](decisions.html#media).

qa.q: Why not expose a signed S3 GET?
qa.a: The application wants current session, selected membership and publication checks when bytes are requested. Server-mediated capability resolution keeps those checks together.
The process-local grant map is lost. The client must obtain a new URL; the film and durable metadata remain in storage.

sections.title: Request path: realtime chat
sections.summary: Messages use HTTP mutations and durable SQL events; server-sent events carry updates to connected members.

steps.label: Send message
steps.detail: The route checks transport, session, selected membership, rate limits, body and optional reply target.

steps.label: Commit
steps.detail: A caller message ID makes matching retries idempotent. The message and ordered event cursor persist before fan-out.

steps.label: Fan out
steps.detail: The route publishes a newly committed event to authorised streams. Reactions use advisory updates plus a snapshot refresh on reconnect.

steps.label: Resume
steps.detail: GET /realtime/groups/:id/events streams updates; persisted message events support replay. The client closes obsolete streams when chat/group context changes.

paragraphs: This is SSE plus normal HTTP, not a WebSocket service. `GET /realtime/groups/:id/messages` supplies bounded history; `POST` on that path sends text. Replies and the supported reaction are separate validated mutations.

The service worker leaves realtime event requests browser-owned so cancellation closes the actual network stream. nginx disables response buffering. Session/group checks also run during stream handling. A SQL event log makes message replay durable, while live subscribers and reaction revisions remain process-local.

qa.q: Why persist events if a live stream exists?
qa.a: The stream can disconnect. Ordered message events let the client resume from a cursor and recover updates it missed.

qa.q: Are reaction events part of that durable cursor?
qa.a: No. Reaction rows persist, but live reaction revisions are advisory. Reconnect refreshes reaction counts without advancing the message/unread cursor.

sections.title: Cross-cutting policy and operations
sections.summary: Every feature shares identity, resource policy, bounded intake and safe operational reporting.

rows: Cognito code + PKCE exchange produces a Rewind opaque session. Web uses a Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax __Host cookie; SQL stores its SHA-256 hash. Idle expiry is 7 days; absolute expiry is 30 days.
Resolve account and profile from the credential; check accepted membership and selected group. Recheck after asynchronous media work. Request group/member IDs cannot grant authority.

Process-local token buckets bound chat, group creation and safety actions; persistent login/invite throttles survive restart. Separate intake, processing, Archive and stream limits bound resource use.
Default JSON 64 KiB; upload-intent and reminder registration bodies 8 KiB; staged photos 10 MiB and clips 50 MiB. Timeouts and bounded rejection handling constrain slow intake.
Responses use stable error codes with user-facing messages. Hidden/unavailable media gets safe denial/not-found responses; uncaught failures become generic errors with request IDs.

Allowlisted session/job/integrity/repair events persist with result/time and sanitised identifiers. Optional request timing logs route templates and SQL timing; raw query values, tokens and message content are excluded. The actor is the signed-in member’s profile id for real-account actions, and null for system or scheduler actions.
Generation-fenced durable job claims, pinned object versions, SHA-256/size receipts and schema readiness stop stale work or altered outputs from being treated as ready.

qa.q: Does checking membership once cover a long upload?
qa.a: No. Asynchronous transfer and probing can outlive the original context. Completion and serving recheck current authority before committing or sending bytes.

qa.q: Does audit record every user action?
qa.a: No. It records a defined set of session, processing and integrity events. Sanitisation also limits stored identifiers; it is not a complete user-activity ledger.

sections.title: Client screens, state and API boundary
sections.summary: The real-account shell composes feature hooks and shared UI; server responses remain the authority for private group state.

rows: App.tsx handles welcome, managed/developer sign-in and display-name onboarding. RealAccountProvider owns session restore, auth state and authenticatedRequest.
src/real contains Home, Film, Archive, Moments, GroupFlows, Shell and Settings. Settings delegates to prompt, timezone, invite, member and account-deletion steps.

RealAccountGroupExperience composes hooks for loading, navigation, membership flows, capture, reminders, ledger and refresh. Context/version refs discard stale asynchronous results after a group change.
src/capture wraps camera/review/upload and platform storage; src/chat wraps history/SSE/reactions/unread; src/reminders wraps subscription and reminder intents.
src/ui provides tokens, fonts, primitives and icons; src/domain provides typed group/cycle/contribution/film contracts. There is no second synthetic app behind real/.

React hooks/context hold screen and session state. API clients use same-origin /api with browser credentials; retained native development uses a bearer token in SecureStore. postJson shares mutation request formatting.

paragraphs: Navigation is composed from shell tabs and pushed feature/settings state in the group hooks. The current shell tabs are Home, Chat and Archive. Capture and Film are feature views controlled by this composition, rather than independent web applications.

The 20 October refactor extracts hooks and panels from the group, video-capture and settings screens. That reduces the orchestration inside large components while preserving the existing HTTP contracts. See [patterns](patterns.html) for the design problems behind these boundaries.

qa.q: What is shared if screens live in real/?
qa.a: The folder names the real-account UI. Shared domain contracts, UI primitives and capture/chat/reminder adapters live in sibling folders; there is no maintained Demo client.

qa.q: How do you avoid showing the old group after switching?
qa.a: Group hooks track context versions and selected-group refs. Late responses from the previous context are discarded, and the server independently checks the selected membership.
